# Actual Tukey facets can have only null-section critical caps

This is a regularity obstruction, not an OC counterexample. Its raw cap
budget is V, whereas the OC target is
Gamma_d(2^n+epsilon)V/2^n<V. No below-target premise is asserted.

Fix n>=2,d>=2, let B be the unit Euclidean d-ball with volume V, choose
0<epsilon<1/2 and r=epsilon^(1/d), and set

    C=conv( ([0,1]^n times B) union ({2e_1} times rB) ).

The integer base set is exactly P={0,1}^n union {2e_1}: each coordinate
except the first lies in [0,1], and the section at first coordinate2
consists only of the added point. At every binary base the fiber is B:
it was inserted, and every convex combination of generating centered
balls has radius at most1. At 2e_1 it is exactly rB by exposedness.
Thus M=(2^n+epsilon)V and EVERY fiber volume is strictly below M/2^n.
Their normalized volumes are uniformly at most1/(2^n+epsilon).

The mixed maximum is exactly (1/2+epsilon)V<V. Every base except e_1
is exposed in conv(P), so finite integer tilts isolate its own ordinary
ball cap; its mixed point-depth function equals its own ball depth.
At e_1, the line fibers at0,e_1,2e_1 are B,B,rB. Reflection of the
small endpoint ball into the large one gives combined endpoint cap
mass at least epsilon V for every through-center continuous direction;
the own ball adds V/2. A finite tilt fills the small endpoint, empties
the large endpoint, and a further negative penalty on sum_(j>=2)z_j
excludes every other binary fiber. This gives equality. The same lift
at any noncentral e_1 point gives epsilon V plus its strictly smaller
own ball depth. Thus (e_1,0) is the unique mixed maximizer.

Let D be the full ambient raw Tukey region at level V. It avoids the
mixed lattice. Its projection has the ACTUAL facet

    F={z_i>=0, sum_i z_i=1/2}.                          (1)

Here is a self-contained verification. Every point (e_i/2,0) has depth
at least V from the centrally symmetric pair of unit-ball fibers at0
and e_i. Convexity of depth superlevels puts F times {0} in D. Conversely
if p has s=sum p_i<1/2, the cap

    u.x >= [sum z_i-s]/(1-s),     ||u||=1,

through (p,0) captures strictly less than V from base0, zero from all
other binary fibers, and zero from the small added ball. Reflection
x->-x preserves the measure, so if any (p,x) belonged to D, convexity
would put (p,0) there too. Thus pi(D) lies in sum z_i>=1/2.

The projection is full dimensional: the simplex on bases0,e_1,...,e_n
alone gives depth at least V at its barycenter g and continuous point0.
More generally, equal centered symmetric fibers at affinely independent
bases give depth at least V at any base barycentric weights <=1/2.
To check this directly, normalize a fixed directional tail as F(t),
where F(-t)=1-F(t), F is strictly decreasing on(-1,1), and is constant
outside. Thresholds satisfy sum lambda_i t_i=0. Two negative thresholds
already give total mass>V. With exactly one negative threshold -L,
its weight<=1/2 implies L>=the smallest nonnegative threshold, so
sum of the nonnegative tails is at least F(L). This gives total>=V.
Consequently g lies in pi(D) away from the plane in(1).

D itself is full dimensional as well. For N=n+1>=3 and inverse ball
tail q:[0,1]->[-1,1], compactness gives

    c_N=min{sum_i q(w_i): w_i>=0, sum_i w_i=1}>0.

Positivity follows as follows. If every w_i<=1/2, all terms are
nonnegative and at least one is positive. If one w_i>1/2, one other
term is at least -q(w_i), and each of the remaining N-2 terms is
strictly positive. The inverse tail is continuous, so the minimum is
attained and positive. A cap through(g,x) of mass<V on those N fibers
would have thresholds with sum t_i=N u.x>=c_N: truncate thresholds
above1 and increase the resulting tail fractions to sum1. This is
impossible for ||x||<c_N/N. Thus a positive continuous ball over g lies
in D; its convex hull with F times{0} has dimension n+d.

Now take p in relint F. Its barycentric weights on0,e_1,...,e_n are
lambda_0=1/2 and lambda_i=p_i>0. In the preceding tail comparison,
EQUALITY at total mass V is possible only when one threshold is <=-1
and every other threshold is >=1. Indeed with two negatives the sum
is strictly greater; with one negative -L and minimum nonnegative t,
if t<1 then F(t)>F(L) when L>t. If L=t, all positive-weight remaining
thresholds equal t and lambda_negative=1/2, giving at least two copies
of the positive number F(t). Hence equality forces t>=1 and L>=1.

Therefore EVERY nonvertical critical through-(p,0) cap captures one
entire unit ball and zero from every other fiber. All its cutting
sections are empty or supporting singletons. Their total H_(d-1)
measure is ZERO. A containing cap not through the source can be shifted
through it; equality forces the same allocation, so this conclusion is
not restricted to a selected menu.

There are explicit full-rank positive-circuit certificates at this
actual projected facet. Choose unit vectors u_j positively spanning R^d
in a minimal d+1 circuit and take

    H_j={u_j.x-2 sum_i z_i>=-1}.

Every H_j has mass V, captures the whole base0 ball, and has zero
capture elsewhere. All its boundaries contain every(p,0) in F times{0}.
The positive continuous-normal dependence gives the projected exterior
sum z_i<=1/2 exactly. These caps support D: shifting any boundary inward
immediately removes positive volume from the captured ball while all
other captures stay zero.

Finally pi(D) lies in [0,1]^n: beyond its first-coordinate upper face a
pure integer cap captures only epsilon V, and beyond any other cube
face such a cap captures zero. Therefore it lies in the explicit
maximal lattice-free crosspolytope

    L={sum_i |z_i-1/2|<=n/2}.

Every integer point has distance at least n/2 from its center. Its2^n
facets have the distinct binary vertices in their relative interiors.
Maximality follows directly: if a point is added beyond one facet,
a small continuation of the segment through that facet's integer
relative-interior witness enters int L, making that witness interior
to the enlarged convex set. The facet sum z_i=0 is parallel to(1).

The normalized critical mass1/(2^n+epsilon) tends to zero with n, and
strict no-heavy volumes do not prevent this zero-section phenomenon.
Its saturated mass credit is explicit: each displayed cap captures a
whole mass V, and its facet exterior owns just that same fiber. The
example does not negate a proof that accounts for this saturated mass;
it negates automatic positive-section regularity at actual contacts.
